paragraphs: Inferring a network from data becomes harder when observations include different data types or come from heterogeneous populations. Traditional Gaussian graphical models are designed around continuous, homogeneous data. Their estimation can also require high-dimensional integration, creating a computational obstacle as the number of variables grows.

The paper introduces a family of graphical models organized around marginal recoverability. This property allows the model to be estimated through its marginal distributions without evaluating the difficult high-dimensional integrals. The framework accommodates Gaussian models, Poisson log-normal models, and latent Gaussian copula models, giving one construction a broader range of applications.

The authors also combine these models into mixtures to represent heterogeneous structures. They establish desirable model properties and effective estimation methods, then evaluate the approach through simulations and a gene regulatory network analysis using single-cell RNA sequencing data. The reported advantages over existing network inference methods support the framework’s combination of flexibility and computational tractability in the settings studied.
icml-2025-a-generic-family-of-graphical-.tldr: A flexible graphical-model family supports diverse data and heterogeneous populations while avoiding high-dimensional integration during estimation.

paragraphs: Predicting material properties with graph neural networks depends on how crystalline structures are converted into graphs. Existing representations are manually designed to respect particular structural symmetry constraints. When new constraints arise, a representation designed for an earlier set may no longer be suitable, making representation construction an obstacle to adapting the prediction method.

Rep-CodeGen addresses this problem by using multiple language-model agents to generate the code that constructs graph representations. Its process has three iterative stages that imitate an evolutionary algorithm. The search therefore operates on representation-building programs, allowing the framework to develop constructions for constraints beyond those handled by its starting code.

The authors report a generated representation satisfying six constraints, starting from code satisfying three. On two real-world material datasets, a property predictor using this representation achieves state-of-the-art performance. This result connects automated code generation to the quality of the resulting scientific representation: the generated programs produce graphs that meet additional constraints and support strong downstream prediction.
icml-2025-code-generated-graph-represent.tldr: Rep-CodeGen uses multiple language-model agents to generate graph-construction code that satisfies new material constraints and improves property prediction.

paragraphs: Online convex optimization involves choosing actions over time while controlling regret, a measure of performance relative to a comparator. This paper studies the setting with a fixed constraint function. Earlier work achieved regret growing as the square root of the number of rounds while ensuring that constraint values summed to a nonpositive total.

That cumulative guarantee can allow a violation at one round to be offset by slack at another. The authors establish the stronger property that every played action satisfies the constraint, while retaining the same order of regret. Their method uses the same kind of constraint information as prior work: the value and a subgradient at played actions.

The algorithm follows each online gradient descent step with a feasibility correction. This correction descends along a constraint subgradient using a Polyak step size. The analysis shows that this additional step can enforce constraints at every round without worsening the stated regret rate. Numerical experiments further validate the approach, linking the theoretical guarantee to its behavior in the tested problems.
icml-2025-constrained-online-convex-opti.tldr: Polyak feasibility corrections enforce constraints at every round of online convex optimization while preserving square-root regret guarantees.

paragraphs: A dynamical system can change qualitatively when a parameter crosses a critical threshold, a phenomenon called bifurcation. Predicting behavior beyond that threshold is difficult because the new regime can differ sharply from the training data. This paper asks whether context-dependent neural ordinary differential equations can nevertheless identify symmetry breaking beyond such a transition.

The authors demonstrate that models trained only on localized, symmetric data before a bifurcation can identify symmetry-breaking behavior afterward, including without examples from the new regime. These models do not require physics-based priors for the demonstrated behavior. The authors interpret this ability through implicit use of topological invariants, particularly the Poincaré index.

A formal explanation based on the Poincaré–Hopf theorem gives conditions under which these models can recover broken symmetries or incorrectly predict them. Thus, the finding is conditional rather than a general guarantee of extrapolation. The authors also develop a topology-based regularizer inspired by the theorem and validate it on phase transitions described by the Landau–Khalatnikov equation.
icml-2025-context-informed-neural-odes-u.tldr: Context-dependent neural ODEs can identify unseen symmetry breaking, with topology explaining conditions for both successful extrapolation and erroneous predictions.

paragraphs: Removing parameters from a language model requires deciding how much to remove from each layer. The paper identifies a problem with this process: reconstruction errors introduced in early layers can propagate and grow in later layers. This accumulation can make the final sparse model substantially less accurate even when individual pruning decisions appear reasonable.

The authors derive an allocation rule in which sparsity increases across layers in an arithmetic progression. Each successive layer receives a fixed increase in sparsity, reducing a many-layer allocation problem to choosing one common-difference hyperparameter. They report that a few trials can identify the best allocation and support the scheme’s near optimality through theory and experiments.

Experiments show improvements across language-model architectures and compression techniques, with applicability also reported for vision and multimodal models. For a 70% sparse LLaMA2-7B model produced with Wanda, the abstract reports a perplexity reduction of 52.10, a 10.50% improvement in average zero-shot accuracy, and CPU and GPU speedups of 2.63 and 2.23 times. These findings show the practical importance of where sparsity is assigned.
icml-2025-determining-layer-wise-sparsit.tldr: Increasing sparsity gradually across layers mitigates amplified reconstruction errors and improves compressed-model performance with a simple allocation rule.

paragraphs: Many-body quantum problems contain symmetries associated with moving multiple objects together. These simultaneous transformations are described by diagonal groups of isometries. Encoding such invariance in a neural network is challenging because, outside special cases, there is no natural choice of a map that removes the irrelevant transformation.

The paper examines three ways to incorporate this structure into neural-network representations trained with variational Monte Carlo: data augmentation, averaging over a group, and canonicalization. Surprisingly, enforcing symmetry during training destabilizes optimization and can worsen performance. The theoretical and numerical analysis suggests that a computational-statistical tradeoff particular to this setting may explain the behavior.

Averaging after training is less sensitive to that tradeoff and is demonstrated as a simple, flexible way to improve the solvers. The distinction matters because symmetry is usually treated as a helpful ingredient to build into training. Here, the results show that the timing and computational form of its incorporation can influence whether it helps the neural solver.
icml-2025-diagonal-symmetrization-of-neu.tldr: For neural quantum solvers, imposing symmetry during training can hurt performance, while averaging after training offers a more effective approach.

paragraphs: DriveGPT approaches autonomous driving as a sequence of decisions. It represents future agent states as tokens and trains a transformer to predict them autoregressively, producing each part of the sequence conditioned on what came before. This formulation creates a behavior model whose capacity and training data can be expanded systematically.

The authors increase both model parameters and dataset size by multiple orders of magnitude. This lets them study how performance relates to model size, data volume, and computation. They evaluate models at different scales on a planning task using quantitative measures and qualitative examples, including closed-loop driving in complex real-world scenarios.

A separate prediction task provides additional evidence about scaling. DriveGPT outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines used in that task, and pretraining on a large dataset further improves performance. The findings support the value of data scaling for this driving representation. The planning evaluations and prediction results address complementary questions: how the model behaves when used for decisions and how accurately it predicts future behavior.
icml-2025-drivegpt-scaling-autoregressiv.tldr: DriveGPT models driving through autoregressive state prediction and finds benefits from scaling training data, including stronger results on a separate prediction task.

paragraphs: A generated program can produce the right answer while taking unnecessarily long to run or consuming excessive memory. This paper addresses the tendency of code-generation training to emphasize correctness without giving comparable attention to execution efficiency. Its proposed approach, SWIFTCODE, builds a fine-tuning dataset containing code selected for both qualities.

Multiple language models generate diverse candidate solutions for programming tasks across different languages. The candidates are executed locally so that their running time and memory use can be measured directly. The method selects solutions with the lowest execution time and memory consumption for the dataset, grounding the efficiency signal in observed program behavior.

Fine-tuning on SWIFTCODE improves both correctness and speed in the reported experiments. For Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, pass@1 rises from 44.8% to 57.7%, while average execution time on correct tasks falls by 48.4%. These results suggest that selecting efficient training examples can improve the programs a model produces, making execution quality part of learning rather than evaluating only whether the output is correct.
icml-2025-efficoder-enhancing-code-gener.tldr: SWIFTCODE fine-tunes code models on correct solutions selected through execution measurements, improving both correctness and runtime in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can adapt to a test image by examining several augmented versions of it. Existing approaches face a performance-efficiency tradeoff: tuning text prompts creates substantial overhead, while handcrafted visual-feature adjustments can provide unstable benefits. GS-Bias introduces a small set of learned corrections intended to make this adaptation effective and inexpensive.

The method learns two biases. A global bias captures the image’s overall semantics by encouraging consistency across augmented views. A spatial bias learns semantic coherence among regions in the image’s visual representation. Both corrections are added directly to the pretrained model’s output logits, avoiding full backpropagation through the vision-language model during adaptation.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance across 15 benchmark datasets. Relative to TPT, the abstract reports improvements of 2.23% in cross-dataset generalization and 2.72% in domain generalization, alongside memory use of only 6.5% of TPT’s on ImageNet. The results indicate that adapting output scores using global and regional information can provide substantial benefits without the computational burden of tuning through the full model.
icml-2025-gs-bias-global-spatial-bias-le.tldr: GS-Bias adapts vision-language predictions with global and spatial output corrections, achieving strong benchmark performance with low memory use.

paragraphs: Learning a sequential task from one video becomes difficult when the demonstrator and learner move at different speeds or have different bodies. Matching individual frames can identify visually similar states without ensuring that the learner completes the task’s stages in order. The paper shows that such matching also fails to ensure consistent progress.

ORCA moves the comparison from individual frames to whole sequences. Its definition of perfect matching requires one sequence to cover the other’s subgoals in the same order. It turns this idea into a dense reward at every timestep, measuring the probability that the agent covers demonstration frames in the correct sequence.

On temporally misaligned demonstrations, ORCA-trained agents achieve 4.5 times the average normalized return on Meta-world and 6.6 times the average return on Humanoid-v4 compared with the best frame-level matching algorithms. Additional empirical analysis shows robustness across different amounts of timing mismatch. These results support using ordered progress as the learning signal when successful imitation should preserve task structure despite differences in execution timing.
icml-2025-imitation-learning-from-a-sing.tldr: ORCA learns from a single video by rewarding ordered coverage of demonstrated subgoals, improving imitation when execution timing differs.

paragraphs: Text-to-audio systems must balance realistic sound with the time needed to generate it. Diffusion models produce high-fidelity audio, but their sampling process can be slow. Iterative masked generation over discrete tokens offers faster inference, yet the abstract identifies an audio-quality gap between that approach and diffusion-based systems.

IMPACT combines iterative mask-based parallel decoding with diffusion modeling in a continuous latent space. Parallel decoding allows multiple parts of the representation to be generated together. Using a continuous representation removes the fidelity constraints associated with discrete tokens, while diffusion supplies the modeling capability used to generate the audio representation.

On AudioCaps, IMPACT achieves state-of-the-art results on key measures including Fréchet Distance and Fréchet Audio Distance, while significantly reducing latency relative to prior models. The stated findings support combining these generation ideas to improve the quality-speed balance. The contribution is the integration of masked parallel decoding and continuous diffusion modeling into a framework that retains competitive inference speed while delivering high audio quality.
icml-2025-impact-iterative-mask-based-pa.tldr: IMPACT combines parallel masked decoding with continuous-space diffusion to improve text-to-audio quality while reducing generation latency.

paragraphs: Language-model recommenders often describe an item identifier using ordinary vocabulary pieces. Those pieces already carry meanings learned from natural language, which can interfere with representing relationships between users and items. This paper studies token construction as a way to make these entities more suitable for recommendation within a language model.

The authors argue for introducing out-of-vocabulary tokens for users and items. They first use representations learned from historical user-item interactions, then cluster them so that combinations with similar properties share tokens. This construction is designed to preserve useful relationships through memorization while maintaining diversity in how users and items are described.

The new tokens are added to the language model’s vocabulary and used during downstream fine-tuning. This gives the model a more suitable way to distinguish recommendation entities and capture their relationships. The proposed framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods across the downstream recommendation tasks evaluated. The results position vocabulary design as an important part of adapting a language model to relational recommendation data.
icml-2025-improving-llms-for-recommendat.tldr: Interaction-based out-of-vocabulary tokens give language models more effective user and item representations for recommendation.

paragraphs: Choosing preference examples for language-model alignment requires deciding which comparisons will be useful for training. Existing selection measures often focus on either an explicit reward margin or an implicit one. Because these describe different aspects of the preference signal, measures based on only one margin can give conflicting assessments of the same example.

The paper proposes alignment potential, a metric that uses both margins. It measures the gap between the model’s current implicit reward margin and the target explicit margin. This makes selection sensitive to how much alignment the particular model could gain from an example, connecting the target preference to the model’s current state.

Across the tested base models and optimization objectives, training on data selected by alignment potential consistently improves alignment relative to existing selection metrics. The authors also apply it to self-play, selecting useful examples from language models’ own generated content. In that setting, the approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods and continues improving as dataset size and training iterations increase in the reported experiments.
icml-2025-larger-or-smaller-reward-margi.tldr: Alignment potential selects preference data by comparing a model’s current reward margin with the target margin, improving alignment in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning depends on producing useful altered versions of a graph. Heuristics such as randomly removing edges can destroy important structure, making performance unstable. PiNGDA studies augmentation as a problem of identifying noise that benefits learning, using an information-theoretic account of why some perturbations help.

To connect this account with the usual contrastive objective, the authors introduce a Gaussian auxiliary variable that expresses the loss in terms of information entropy. They prove that standard graph contrastive learning with predefined augmentations corresponds to a point estimate of beneficial noise. This interpretation provides a theoretical basis for changing how augmentation noise is obtained.

PiNGDA uses a trainable generator to learn perturbations of both graph topology and node attributes. The augmentation mechanism can therefore learn how to alter connections and features in beneficial ways. Extensive experiments support the method’s effectiveness and stability. The findings connect the theoretical treatment of noise to a practical augmentation strategy, with reported reliability improvements over existing methods that rely on simpler augmentation estimates.
icml-2025-learn-beneficial-noise-as-grap.tldr: PiNGDA learns beneficial perturbations to graph connections and node features, improving the effectiveness and stability of graph contrastive learning.

paragraphs: Visual reinforcement learning lets robots acquire skills from images, but learning can require too much experience to be practical. MENTOR addresses this sample-efficiency problem by changing both the agent’s network architecture and its optimization. The aim is to make visual learning more effective for robotic tasks in unstructured settings.

Architecturally, MENTOR replaces a standard multilayer perceptron with a mixture-of-experts backbone, organizing the network around multiple expert components. It also introduces a task-oriented perturbation mechanism as part of the learning approach. These two changes address how the agent represents its decision process and how that process is optimized during training.

MENTOR outperforms state-of-the-art methods on three simulation benchmarks. Across three challenging real-world manipulation tasks, it reaches an average success rate of 83%, compared with 32% for the strongest existing model-free visual reinforcement-learning algorithm in the comparison. The results provide evidence that the combined architecture and optimization approach can improve practical robotic performance, alongside the paper’s broader focus on making better use of learning experience.
icml-2025-mentor-mixture-of-experts-netw.tldr: MENTOR combines a mixture-of-experts backbone with task-oriented perturbation to improve visual reinforcement learning and real-world robotic manipulation.

paragraphs: A team of language-model agents can benefit from specialization, but an agent that repeatedly makes mistakes can undermine the group. This paper examines how communication structure affects resilience to faulty agents, including agents intended to simulate clumsy or malicious behavior. It also studies mechanisms for detecting and correcting their contributions.

The authors introduce AutoTransform and AutoInject to place mistakes into agent responses. Across four downstream tasks and six systems, a hierarchical arrangement, with one agent feeding into two interacting agents, has the smallest reported performance decline: 5.5%. The other two structures show declines of 10.5% and 23.7%, indicating that organization affects error resilience in these experiments.

Two additional defenses improve resilience. Challenger allows agents to question one another’s outputs, while Inspector adds an agent that reviews and corrects messages. The paper reports recovery of up to 96.4% of errors made by faulty agents. Together, the results show that communication design and explicit review mechanisms are practical factors in maintaining collaborative performance when some participants produce incorrect information.
icml-2025-on-the-resilience-of-llm-based.tldr: Hierarchical communication and explicit challenge or inspection mechanisms improve language-model teams’ resilience to faulty agents in the tested settings.

paragraphs: Language-model scaling usually invites questions about model size and training data, but the vocabulary also shapes what the model receives. This paper investigates scaling the input vocabulary as a route to improved language modeling. Its Over-Tokenized Transformer framework separates the vocabularies used for input and output, allowing the input side to grow independently.

The expanded input vocabulary includes multi-gram tokens, representing groups of tokens as input units. Across extensive experiments, the authors find a log-linear relationship between input vocabulary size and training loss. Larger input vocabularies consistently improve performance across the model sizes studied, making vocabulary size an additional dimension to consider in scaling.

With a large input vocabulary, the method achieves performance comparable to baselines twice its size, with no additional cost as reported in the abstract. These findings suggest that input representation can materially affect the performance available from a model. They also motivate tokenizer design that considers the benefits of input-vocabulary expansion separately from decisions about the output vocabulary.
icml-2025-over-tokenized-transformer-voc.tldr: Separating input and output vocabularies lets transformers benefit from larger multi-gram input vocabularies, improving performance across the tested model sizes.

paragraphs: An agent that observes only part of its environment can struggle to recognize both opportunities and dangers. This makes partial observability especially challenging for safe reinforcement learning. The paper studies how privileged information available during training can help address these difficulties and improve the agent’s learned behavior.

The authors introduce Asymmetric Constrained Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes as a theoretical framework for examining this use of information. They then build PIGDreamer, a model-based reinforcement-learning method, on that framework. Its two highlighted mechanisms are privileged representation alignment and an asymmetric actor-critic structure, which incorporate the training information into how the agent learns representations and behavior.

The experiments report significant improvements over existing safe reinforcement-learning methods. Compared with alternative methods that also use privileged information, PIGDreamer shows better performance, robustness, and efficiency. These findings support the particular way PIGDreamer integrates additional training information, beyond the general idea of making that information available. The contribution combines a formal setting for studying the asymmetry with an implemented learning method that shows empirical benefits.
icml-2025-pigdreamer-privileged-informat.tldr: PIGDreamer uses privileged training information to improve safe reinforcement learning under partial observability, with gains in performance, robustness, and efficiency.

paragraphs: The paper asks how much sampled graph data is needed to detect whether two graphs are correlated when their vertices have no known correspondence. Both graphs follow the Gaussian Wigner model. The unknown correspondence is represented by a hidden vertex permutation, which makes detecting their relationship more difficult.

The authors formulate the problem as a hypothesis test. Under the null hypothesis, the graphs are independent; under the alternative, their edges are correlated through the hidden permutation. Each graph has the same marginal distribution in both cases, so the distinction lies in their joint relationship. The observation setting consists of two sampled induced subgraphs, each with a fixed number of vertices.

Using a conditional second-moment analysis, the paper establishes the optimal rate for the sample size needed to detect correlation in this setting. It also proposes an efficient approximate algorithm that substantially reduces running time. The contributions address both the statistical question of how much information detection requires and the computational question of carrying out an approximate procedure efficiently.
icml-2025-sample-complexity-of-correlati.tldr: The paper establishes an optimal sample-size rate for detecting correlation between unlabeled Gaussian Wigner graphs and proposes a faster approximate algorithm.

paragraphs: Inductive knowledge graph completion predicts missing relationships in a graph different from the one used for training. Subgraph reasoning models have performed well empirically on this task, but their ability to transfer raises a theoretical question: how does sensitivity to changes in local graph structure relate to the gap between training and test performance?

The paper defines stability through the consistency of a model’s outputs when its input subgraphs differ. To measure those input differences, the authors introduce Relational Tree Mover’s Distance. This supplies a way to relate changes in relational graph structure to changes in the predictions produced by a subgraph reasoning model.

The analysis establishes a proportional relationship between the stability quantity and generalization, expressed as the discrepancy between training and test performance. Experiments on real-world datasets examine the effect of stability and validate the theoretical findings. The contribution gives a formal account of an observed modeling concern: understanding transfer to a new knowledge graph requires examining how predictions respond to differences in the subgraphs used for reasoning.
icml-2025-stability-and-generalization-c.tldr: A theoretical analysis connects subgraph reasoning models’ sensitivity to structural changes with their training-to-test generalization gap.

paragraphs: Protein language models learn from large collections of natural protein sequences, but directing them toward precisely specified properties remains challenging. This paper investigates activation steering as a way to control their outputs. The technique adapts an approach developed for text language models to the generation and optimization of protein sequences.

The proposed method edits internal activations to steer the model toward targeted properties. The authors also extend the approach to protein optimization through a module that identifies editing sites. This adds a mechanism for deciding where edits should be directed when using the model to improve a protein sequence.

Experiments focus on generating and optimizing lysozyme-like sequences. The authors demonstrate integration with both auto-encoding and autoregressive protein language models without additional training. That compatibility matters because the control mechanism can be applied across these two model families without retraining them for the steering procedure. The stated results present activation editing as a promising route toward more precise protein engineering, with the empirical evidence centered on the sequence tasks studied.
icml-2025-steering-protein-language-mode.tldr: Activation editing steers protein language models toward targeted properties and supports sequence optimization without additional training.

paragraphs: This paper studies stochastic nonconvex optimization with linear inequality constraints. The challenge combines noisy gradient information, a nonconvex objective, and the need to satisfy constraints. The proposed algorithms use a single loop and require only one or two stochastic gradient samples per iteration, keeping each update comparatively simple.

The central construction treats the algorithm as inexact gradient descent on a Moreau envelope, a smoothed optimization object. Its gradient is estimated using one step of a stochastic primal-dual augmented Lagrangian algorithm. The analysis combines global error bounds for constrained optimization with a Moreau-envelope treatment of stochastic proximal methods to handle inequalities and noise together.

The authors establish sample-complexity rates of O(ε⁻⁴) and O(ε⁻³), each optimal in its respective case, and extend the approach to stochastic linear constraints. The iterations avoid subproblems, large batches, and increasing penalty parameters; dual-variable updates provide the mechanism for ensuring feasibility. The contribution pairs these theoretical efficiency guarantees with an algorithmic structure that avoids several sources of expensive work inside each iteration.
icml-2025-stochastic-smoothed-primal-dua.tldr: Single-loop primal-dual algorithms achieve case-specific optimal sample complexity for stochastic nonconvex problems with linear inequality constraints.

paragraphs: Long-term forecasting can become expensive when models use many parameters to represent dependencies across time. TimeBase starts from the observation that time series often contain similar temporal patterns and low-rank structure, particularly over long horizons. These properties suggest that a compact representation may capture much of the useful forecasting information.

The method extracts core temporal basis components and changes the forecasting unit from individual points to segments. Together, these choices direct the network toward a concise representation of the time series and reduce the complexity of producing long forecasts. The architecture is designed to make efficient use of both the data and its parameters.

Experiments on diverse real-world datasets show strong efficiency with competitive forecasting performance. The abstract also reports that TimeBase can act as a plug-and-play complexity reducer for patch-based forecasting models. This gives the method two roles: an ultralightweight forecaster in its own right and a way to simplify other forecasting systems. The results support exploiting recurring temporal structure when seeking lower computational cost without losing competitive accuracy.
icml-2025-timebase-the-power-of-minimali.tldr: TimeBase uses compact temporal components and segment-level forecasting to achieve strong efficiency with competitive long-term forecasting performance.

paragraphs: Language models can simulate survey answers, but their responses may follow a different distribution from those of the target human population. This paper studies how to turn imperfect simulated responses into confidence sets for human population parameters. The central concern is making the uncertainty reflect that mismatch rather than treating simulated answers as interchangeable with human answers.

The number of simulated responses creates a tradeoff. Too many can produce confidence sets that are overly narrow and fail to cover the target adequately; too few produce loose estimates. The proposed method selects the simulation sample size adaptively and establishes valid average-case coverage guarantees. This qualification concerns coverage on average, rather than an unconditional guarantee for every individual survey setting.

The approach applies to any language model, regardless of its fidelity, and to any confidence-set construction procedure. The selected sample size also quantifies misalignment between the model and the human population. Illustrations using real datasets and language models show how sample-size selection can serve both uncertainty quantification and assessment of the simulation’s population mismatch.
icml-2025-uncertainty-quantification-for.tldr: Adaptively choosing how many survey responses to simulate yields average-case coverage guarantees while quantifying mismatch with the human population.

paragraphs: A quantum machine-learning model needs to perform well on new data as well as its training examples. This paper addresses weaknesses in existing ways of reasoning about that generalization, particularly theories based on uniform bounds. It proposes a margin-based generalization bound as a more reliable framework for evaluating quantum models.

The approach uses margins to characterize generalization rather than relying only on broad measures of model complexity. Experiments on a quantum phase recognition dataset show that margin-based metrics strongly predict generalization performance and outperform traditional measures such as parameter count. This provides empirical support for the proposed theoretical perspective in the studied recognition task.

The authors also connect the margin-based metric to quantum information theory. Through that connection, they demonstrate a classical-quantum hybrid approach that improves generalization when quantum machine learning is applied to classical data. The contribution therefore links explanation and improvement: margins help assess how well a model will transfer beyond training data, and their quantum-information interpretation provides a route to enhancing that behavior.
icml-2025-understanding-generalization-i.tldr: Margin-based theory and metrics better explain quantum-model generalization in the reported experiments and motivate a hybrid method for improving it.
